schools.summary: Clarke marks that the poetry of the book begins here (the prior chapters being prose), hears the execration as awfully solemn and sublime yet the fruit of a mind in heaviness; Wesley judges the curse sinful — vain, aimed at a thing that cannot be cursed, and casting blame on God — though Job stops short of cursing God.
Henry calls the curse Job's infirmity, unjustifiable yet excusable in part, insisting on the limit: Job cursed his day but not his God, weary of life but not of his religion.
Gill reads 'opened his mouth' as simply breaking the long seven-day silence.
Ellicott compares Jeremiah 20:14-18 and argues Job is the original, indispensable to the poem, Jeremiah quoting it as a passing mood.
Gregory the Great counsels that the harsh literal words, seeming to contradict, direct the reader to a deeper truth to be sought beneath the surface.

debates.question: Is the chapter's likeness to Jeremiah 20:14-18 a borrowing, and which is original?

sides.position: Job is the original; Jeremiah quotes it as the record of a passing mood
neither borrowed from the other — a common Asiatic mode of thought and speech

themes: curse the day but not God

schools.summary: Gill notes 'answered and said' though none had spoken — Job answers his own calamity and their silence — and that the book now turns to a poetical Hebrew metre, obscure even to the Jews, one Targum reading 'Job sang and said.'

Keil and Delitzsch take 'answered' as beginning to speak from a prior incitement (like the NT 'answered'), the point where the poetic accentuation begins, and lay out the speech's three-fold movement while denying it is strophic in any strict sense.

debates.question: Are the three movements of the speech true strophes?

sides.position: yes — three strophes or parts (cursing life, longing for death, reproachful inquiry)
holders: Schlottmann (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
Hahn (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: no — a progress of feeling, not a measured stanza-form

themes: the three-fold movement of the lament

schools.summary: Gill offers both senses — that Job wishes he had never been born, or that his birthday be struck from the calendar and kept with no solemnity — to show the greatness of his affliction.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the curse on the birthday and night of conception as recurring yearly (against Schlottmann's actual first day), and read the personified night as itself the speaker that reported the conception to the High One.
Clarke argues the word 'conceived' should here be taken as 'born,' since the night of conception could not be known or published; Wesley reads it as a wish that the day's remembrance be utterly lost.

debates.question: Does the second line speak of conception or of birth?

sides.position: conception — the night that witnessed the man-child conceived
birth — the word should be taken as 'born,' conception being unknowable

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses 'regard' as literally 'require, ask for, care about' (cf. Deut. 11:12); Keil and Delitzsch render 'let not Eloah ask after it,' a dies ater unsought by God.
Clarke reads it as 'blotted out of the calendar' — let God not require it as part of the year, nor the light distinguish it; Wesley wishes the sun had never risen on it.
Gill insists the darkness is literal and gross, not the figure of calamity — the reverse of the creating 'let there be light.'
Henry has Job wish heaven would frown on his day, marked as with a black coal for an evil day by him who orders the times, left to want the benefit of both greater and lesser lights.

Ellicott reads 'stain' as literally 'redeem — claim as their rightful inheritance' (cf. Isa. 63:3; Mal. 1:7) and 'blackness of the day' as preternatural darkness like an eclipse; Keil and Delitzsch render 'may darkness and the shadow of death purchase it back.'

Clarke derives the verb from the goel, the kinsman-avenger, glossing 'pollute or avenge it,' with the cloud as the storehouse of the densest vapours and the Targum's day of national calamity (Jeremiah's grief, Jonah, Egypt's darkness); Wesley reads the shadow of death and 'stain' as taking away the day's beauty, a frightful day terrifying men in it.
Gill records both the darkness of death staining the day and the alternative 'let them redeem it,' claiming it so light have no share in it.

debates.question: How should the disputed verb behind 'stain it' be rendered?

sides.position: pollute or avenge it — from the root of the goel, the avenger of blood
redeem, claim, or purchase it back as a rightful inheritance
stain it — take away its beauty and glory

themes: darkness and the shadow of death

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects 'let it not be joined' to 'let it not rejoice among' the days of the year, as one of the glorious procession of nights; Keil and Delitzsch read the same, denying the night any share in the gladness of the ordered times.

Clarke follows the Targum ('let it not be reckoned among the festivals') and notes the personification of day, night, darkness, and cloud, some taking the word as a dark storm or whirlwind; Wesley reads a constant darkness with no moon or star, the night not reckoned as one of the year's days.
Gill marks the turn to the night of conception, on which Job now imprecates evils.
Henry sets the verse under Job's wish that earth forget his birth, the calendar itself refusing to own the night.

debates.question: Should the middle clause read 'be joined' or 'rejoice among' the days of the year?

sides.position: joined / reckoned as one of the year's days
rejoice among the days of the year, as a festal company

schools.summary: Gill reads 'solitary' as barren and desolate — no company, feasts, or marriage, and (with R. Simeon) no children born, barren as a flint.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'let that night become barren,' childless and fruitless of gladness.

Clarke traces the word to an Arabic root (cut off, bare, a rock), glossing 'grievous, oppressive, as destitute of good as a bare rock is of verdure,' and reports the Targum's 'let there be tribulation' and the silenced wild cock.
Henry sets it under Job's wish that joy forsake his night — a melancholy night, not a merry one, with no joyful voice.

sides.position: barren and childless, empty of the children and feasts that gladden other nights
grievous and oppressive, hard and bare as a stripped rock

schools.summary: Clarke renders 'them who are ready to raise up the leviathan' — desperate men who provoke the crocodile — and rejects the sorcerer reading (Schultens) as unworthy of Job, reporting Calmet's Atlantes; Wesley keeps 'their mourning,' the professional mourners full of sorrow, bidding them curse Job's day.

Ellicott takes the cursers as those who proclaim days unlucky, ready to arouse leviathan or the crocodile, as mad and reckless as that; Keil and Delitzsch render 'who are skilled in stirring up leviathan.'
Gill offers several cursers of the day — adulterers and murderers who hate light, the Ethiopians who curse the sun, or hired funeral mourners.
Henry holds both readings — funeral mourners raising lamentation, or those who curse leviathan (the whale or crocodile) by incantation, or, with Bishop Patrick, conjurers raising the devil.

debates.question: Does the clause read 'raise up their mourning' or 'rouse up leviathan'?

sides.position: 'their mourning' — hired mourners full of sorrow, bidden to curse the day
'rouse up leviathan' — desperate men who stir up the crocodile
holds both readings possible
the crocodile or whale, roused by reckless and desperate men
the devil, raised by the curses of conjurers

outliers.note: Reports Calmet's view that the Ethiopian Atlantes are meant, who curse the sun and hunt the crocodile, and calls it a good sense.

themes: let them curse it that curse the day

schools.summary: Ellicott gives 'the dawning' literally as 'the eyelids of the dawn'; Keil and Delitzsch render the night longing for a light it never finds, unrefreshed by the eyelids of the morning.

Clarke identifies the twilight stars with the planets and reads a sustained personification — darkness waiting in vain for evening star and dawn; Wesley draws out the poetic fiction of a night made to 'look' for light and be disappointed, the eyelids of the day being the morning-star.
Gill takes the twilight for the evening dusk, its stars denied so the night has no relief or guidance for travellers.
Henry has Job wish his night so long it never sees the eyelids of the morning, which bring joy.
Gill reads 'the doors of my womb' of the mother's womb (against Aben Ezra's navel), the night blamed for not closing it — Job avoiding the name of God, to whom closing the womb is elsewhere ascribed.

Clarke refuses to make Job wish his mother destroyed, following the Targum's umbilical cord — had it been shut, a miscarriage, and sorrow hidden from his eyes; Wesley reads simply that the night did not keep him from this miserable life.
Henry finds here the ground of Job's quarrel, and the folly of a passionate discontent that undervalues the noble gift of being because it came clogged with trouble.

debates.question: Does the verse wish the womb had been Job's grave (his mother's death)?

sides.position: the plain reading — the doors of the womb should have stayed shut, even to being his grave
the humaner reading — the umbilical cord shut, sorrow hidden without the mother's death

schools.summary: Gill: since his conception was not hindered, Job wishes he had died in the womb or the moment he left it.
Clarke reads three deaths in view — abortion, still-birth, and dying shortly after birth — Job meaning each in turn.
Keil and Delitzsch note the perfect and future carry the force of the subjunctive, Job imagining a death that mercifully was not.
Henry rebukes the ingratitude yet turns it to a meditation on infant frailty and the mercy that we 'died not from the womb,' owed not to our strength but to God's power and pity.

themes: why died I not from the womb

schools.summary: Clarke reads the dandling on the knees and nursing at the breast; Wesley calls the nurse's care a 'cruel kindness' that betrayed Job into life, and says he unthankfully despises God's mercies to helpless infants.
Gill takes the knees for the midwife's or the father's (the ancient custom of owning a child, cf. the goddess Levana), not the mother's as Jarchi held.
Ellicott glosses 'prevent': why was he nursed with care instead of being left to fall to the ground and be killed.
Henry: the lamp of life would go out but for the breasts, natural affection being put into parents' hearts by the God of nature.

sides.position: the midwife's, or the father's who owned the child on his knees
the mother's

themes: the breasts that I should suck

schools.summary: Gill draws the comparison of the grave to a bed, only more restful, free from the tossing and pain that now beset him.
Clarke reads the four verbs as an ascending calm — insensible, quiet, asleep, at rest, out of the reach of calamity.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'so should I now have lain and had quiet,' the word 'now' measuring his torment by the peace he pictures losing.
Henry hears the poverty of the hope — Job dreams only of the body's quiet, whereas submission might have given his soul rest even now (Ps. 25:13).

themes: then should I have lain still
the grave as a bed of rest
the body's quiet and the soul's

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'desolate places' as gorgeous tombs and sepulchres, desolate because tenanted only by the dead (possibly the Pyramids), or places now ruined; Keil and Delitzsch render 'who built ruins for themselves.'

Clarke takes them for sepulchral monuments, mausoleums, and pyramids, expressly rejecting the reading that makes them princes repairing ruins; Wesley takes the opposite, men who rebuilt ruined cities or raised palaces in the waste.
Gill: death spares neither the power of kings nor the wisdom of counsellors, levelling them with all others, even with children who died at birth.
Henry embraces both tombs and buried treasure and turns all to one lesson — death an irresistible leveller, mingling sceptres with spades.

debates.question: What are the 'desolate places' the great built for themselves?

sides.position: tombs, mausoleums, and pyramids — sepulchres desolate because peopled only by the dead
cities and palaces rebuilt or raised in waste and solitary places

schools.summary: Gill: princes whose greatness lay in gold and silver, now level with those who had none, their wealth neither preserving them nor remaining theirs.
Clarke: mighty men who got gold and filled their houses with silver, yet left all behind, keeping only the empty grave they had made — with Saady's proverb of the covetous filled at last with dust.
Keil and Delitzsch set the gold-rich princes beside the kings of the preceding verse as another rank the grave equalizes.
Henry: not even princes with gold could bribe Death, and they left their silver-filled houses, no more to return.

themes: the dust that fills the covetous

schools.summary: Gill renders 'hid, as one born out of time' (the apostle's word, 1 Cor. 15:8), an abortive birth like fruit fallen unripe, hidden in the womb or from sight.

Clarke distinguishes the early miscarriage (never having a human form) from infants farther advanced yet miscarried; Wesley glosses 'hidden' as undiscerned and born before the due time, never come into the land of the living.
Ellicott notes another of the conditions Job names that would have relieved him from suffering.
Henry sets the untimely birth at the climax of the grave's equality, lying as safe as kings and princes because it never knew sorrow.

themes: the abortive lies as safe as kings

schools.summary: Clarke sets the toils of the mighty against the labours of the slave, both ended in the grave; Wesley: the great oppressors cease their vexations, rapines, and murders, and the molested sleep beside them.

Ellicott notes 'there' means the grave, indicated but unnamed; Keil and Delitzsch render 'the wicked cease from troubling, and the weary are at rest,' the roots carrying restless commotion and perfect freedom from care.
Gill: the wicked, restless as the troubled sea, can do no mischief in the grave, and the good man is troubled no more by wicked men, his own heart, or Satan.
Henry: persecutors who die can persecute no more (Herod ceased when the worms took him), and the weary rest from their labours (Rev. 14:13), though Job dreams only of the body's rest.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'the captives dwell together in tranquillity, they hear not the voice of the taskmaster'; Ellicott notes the word for 'oppressor' is the 'taskmaster' of the Exodus, hinting an allusion (cf. Exod. 5:6).

Clarke reads the oppressor as the hard taskmaster whose voice was worse than death, silenced now in the dust, and hears a possible echo of the Egyptian bondage; Wesley limits the scene to freedom from worldly troubles, not the eternal state.
Gill: prisoners for debt, the galleys, or religion have their chains knocked off, at ease with fellow-prisoners and even their jailers.
Henry: death is the prisoner's discharge and the servant's manumission, no more put to grind in the prison-house nor terrified by taskmasters.

themes: the grave a jubilee for the captive

schools.summary: Gill: small and great, whether in age, stature, or estate, come to the grave without distinction, 'little and great' all one.

Clarke makes it a set-piece on human equality — all reduced to common dust, the grave the rendezvous where all travellers meet — crowned with Horace and Seneca on death that manumits the slave; Wesley draws the moral for the powerful to rule moderately and the subject to bear patiently.
Henry: the small and great are there all one, the pomp of the great and the wants of the low alike ended, for death and the grave know no difference.

themes: the small and great are there
the servant free from his master

schools.summary: Clarke: why is life granted to one incapable of enjoying it; Wesley: light is the light of life, given because daily renewed, and 'bitter' names those to whom life itself is a burden.
Gregory the Great sets behind the complaint the hidden problem of why it is sometimes ill with the good and well with the wicked, God's appointments deeply concealed.
Gill reads 'light' as the light of the living, and hears a reverent 'wherefore does he give light?' — God meant but unnamed, that Job not seem to quarrel with him.
Henry: life is candle-light, given and daily renewed, but to the miserable a 'gift and no gift,' serving only to show them their own misery.
Ellicott notes the deliberate pairing of light and life (cf. Ps. 36:9; John 1:4).

themes: life to the bitter in soul
the problem of the suffering righteous

schools.summary: Gill: they gape for death as the hungry for food, yet it comes not, its time not being come; death may be lawfully desired by good men, but with submission and patience.

Clarke: they long for death as the end of misery, more than gold-lovers for a mine; Wesley marks that Job durst do nothing to hasten his death, waiting his appointed time till his change came (Job 14:14).
Keil and Delitzsch render the longing as a digging after death more eager than the search for buried treasure.
Henry notes the verse assumes no thought of self-murder, else the longing need not dig so hard for what it could soon reach.

themes: long for death but it comes not
dig for it as for treasure

schools.summary: Gill (with Broughton) renders 'joy till they do skip again,' so elated at the grave they leap for joy.
Clarke notes a Kennicott variant turning 'with joy' into 'at the tomb'; Wesley draws the moral that such impatience of life is unnatural and ungrateful to the Giver of life.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'who rejoice with exceeding joy, who are enraptured, when they can find the grave.'
Henry sets it as the last of Job's three postures — longing, digging, and bidding death welcome, glad to step into the grave.

themes: rejoice when they find the grave

schools.summary: Gill offers two senses of 'whose way is hid' — hidden from God (Job's cause overlooked) or the way of God hidden from Job, who sees no reason for his troubles.
Clarke: one who knows not what is before him, hedged about so he cannot escape (cf. Lam. 3:7); Wesley: the way hid from Job, put as in a prison with no way out.
Ellicott catches the irony that the same 'hedged in' was used in the opposite, protective sense of Job 1:10 — the shelter turned prison.
Henry: Job saw no way of deliverance, his path hedged with thorns, his grief that he knew not why God contended with him.

debates.question: In what sense is Job's 'way hid'?

sides.position: his way hidden from God — his cause overlooked and unregarded
the way of God hidden from Job — he cannot see why God contends with him

themes: he knew not why God contended

schools.summary: Clarke reads the sighing as taking away all appetite and serving in place of meat (cf. Ps. 42:3), the roarings like a swollen torrent; Wesley: all the time he eats he sighs and weeps, his roarings loud outcries poured out like waters that break their banks.
Gill takes it temporally — before he tastes his food there is nothing but sighing, and his tears mingle with the meal.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'instead of my food my sighing cometh,' the particle passing from local to substitutionary (like Latin pro, cf. Job 4:19).
Henry: his sorrows returned as duly as his meals, affliction his daily bread, his roarings poured out like waters in a constant stream.

debates.question: Does the first line read 'before I eat' or 'instead of my food'?

sides.position: temporal — the sighing comes before or during the meal
substitutionary — sighing comes instead of food

themes: my sighing comes before I eat

schools.summary: Ellicott (cf. Prov. 28:14): Job kept in mind the instability of earthly things yet was overtaken by a calamity that mocked his carefulness and exceeded his fears; Keil and Delitzsch render 'I fear something terrible, and it cometh upon me.'

Clarke ('I feared a fear'): in prosperity he dreaded loss of family and property, and both came, yet he was 'not lifted up,' knowing all was from Providence; Wesley: even in prosperity he was full of fears, and those fears are now justified.
Gill doubts a man of Job's faith would indulge such fears, and will not read the verse of his former life in prosperity at all.
Henry: Job's blameless vigilance — afraid for his children when feasting (Job 1:5) — could not keep the trouble off.

debates.question: Did Job in his prosperity really harbour such fears of adversity?

sides.position: yes — in his ease he foresaw and dreaded loss, and it came upon him
no — a man of Job's faith would not so indulge fear; not to be read of his prosperity

themes: vigilance that could not avert the blow

schools.summary: Clarke reads it as a question — 'was I not in safety? yet trouble came' — of his former prosperity, one wave following another (cf. Ps. 42:7), noting Good's 'I had no peace'; Wesley: 'I did not misbehave in prosperity, but walked humbly with God,' yet his way was hid.
Gill holds the words cannot refer to his prosperity, when God's hedge kept him safe; the unrest belongs to his present estate.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'I dwelt not in security, nor rested, nor refreshed myself: then trouble cometh,' the present tense letting the calamity break in.
Henry reconciles both: even in prosperity Job was never careless or secure, kept his guard, trusted not in wealth — yet trouble came, to convince him of the world's vanity.

debates.question: Does v.26 describe Job's former prosperity or deny he ever had peace?

sides.position: it recalls his prosperity and peace — 'was I not in safety? yet trouble came'
it cannot refer to his prosperity (then he was safe under God's hedge); or 'I had no peace'
